scientificFindings.reason: For each disaccharide, actual expansion yields 12 carbons and 11 oxygens (23 heavy atoms), 22 explicitly accounted hydrogens, eight hydroxyl oxygens, two ring oxygens and one shared glycosidic oxygen. Every C has valence four and every O valence two. Each graph is connected with two rings; no atoms need an external structure lookup.

All ten stereogenic ring carbons of the shown alpha maltose anomer and all nine in sucrose have explicit up/down assignments in an explicit ring viewing convention. The glucose down/up/down oxygen sequence, D-C5 hydroxymethyl side, alpha glucose glycosidic positions and beta fructose C2-Og side agree with the named sugars. Fructose C2 has zero H and two separately attached terminal CH2OH carbons are present.

scientificFindings.aspect: usable representation and no answer substitution
scientificFindings.reason: The tabulated material supplies ring connectivity, numbered carbon positions, all substituents and stereo sides; it can be read or reconstructed without obtaining a missing structure. It does not mark which compound gives a positive or negative assay or label the free centre as the answer. It is structured textual chemical material, not a newly inspected learner-facing raster Haworth image. No UI/V publication acceptance is implied.

Under the explicitly equal alkaline copper assay and absence of prior acidic hydrolysis, the learner can independently identify the right maltose hemiacetal C1 as free and both sucrose anomeric centres as glycosidically bound, connect ring opening to accessible reducing chemistry and reject sugar-unit count as explanation. Showing alpha maltose does not remove its reducing end.

The unchanged positive alkaline free-fructose case changes from glycosidic-centre availability in disaccharides to condition-dependent aldose/ketose interconversion. Keto-enol rearrangement explains why the ketose need not test negative. This is a chemically changed case, not a number swap or a claim that bound sucrose hydrolyses in the case-a conditions.
